name: Time as numbered motion
plain_explanation: Aristotle argues time is not nothing (though it is made of a no-longer-existing past and a not-yet-existing future), but rather 'motion that admits of numeration' -- and, curiously, he wonders whether time could exist at all without a soul present to do the counting.
precise_definition: Aristotle's account of time (in the Physics) as a countable aspect of motion, raising the puzzle of whether time can exist independently of a mind capable of numeration, since counting seems to require a counter; Aristotle also holds that motion, and hence time, has always existed and always will, in explicit disagreement with Plato, who held time was created.
why_it_mattered: It set up a direct point of conflict for later Christian Aristotelians, who were obliged to dissent from Aristotle's eternal-universe view since scripture holds that the universe had a beginning.
historical_origin: Developed in the Physics, following the discussion of motion and preceding the argument for an unmoved mover.
examples: 'There always has been motion, and there always will be; for there cannot be time without motion, and all are agreed that time is uncreated, except Plato.'
competing_positions: Plato's view (noted as the sole exception among ancient philosophers) that time was created.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Created a direct doctrinal conflict for medieval Christian Aristotelians, who had to reject Aristotle's eternal-universe doctrine on biblical grounds.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly conflicted with the Christian doctrine of a created, temporally finite universe.
